summary: Background: Digital nursing technologies (DNTs) have the potential to improve the quality and continuity of home care by supporting nurses, care recipients, and informal caregivers. Despite growing research on DNTs, the home care setting remains underrepresented, particularly regarding implementation strategies using an established implementation science framework. Therefore, this scoping review systematically maps implementation strategies for DNTs in home care using the Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change (ERIC) framework. Objective: We aimed to identify and map ERIC implementation strategies proposed or used for DNTs in home care. Additionally, we aimed to derive operationalized practical recommendations for decision-makers and implementation practitioners in nursing services. Methods: We conducted a scoping review with a systematic literature search in MEDLINE via PubMed, CINAHL via EBSCO, and Scopus via Elsevier in March 2025, with an updated search in July 2026. Guided by the PCC (Population, Concept, and Context) framework, we included primary studies and study protocols that addressed the implementation of a DNT in home care and were published between 2015 and 2026. We excluded studies from other health care settings, technologies not related to nursing, concept papers, and reviews. Data charting was conducted in MAXQDA 24 (VERBI Software) using deductive content analysis. We applied and operationalized the 73 ERIC implementation strategies to define our deductive category system. Results: A total of 22 articles with 18 distinct DNTs were included in this review. Most of them are implementation studies conducted in Europe and published in 2022. Most DNTs focused on home care using sensor-based monitoring and telehealth solutions for people with dementia, chronic conditions, or palliative care needs. Additional DNTs included mobile apps for symptom monitoring, decision-support systems, communication platforms, and a robotic medication management system. Deductive analysis based on the ERIC framework identified 48 of 73 implementation strategies across the included DNTs. The most frequently reported ERIC strategies were: conduct educational meetings (n=14), promote adaptability (n=14), conduct ongoing training (n=9), and train-the-trainer (n=9). The identified ERIC implementation strategies showed high heterogeneity across the included DNTs. Conclusions: These frequently reported ERIC implementation strategies may function as a multifaceted implementation strategy. However, they need to be empirically evaluated regarding their feasibility, appropriateness, and effectiveness for the implementation of DNTs in home care. In addition, researchers should ensure transparent reporting of implementation strategies by explicitly operationalizing them and applying established frameworks, such as the ERIC framework, to facilitate comparability across studies. Finally, practical guidance derived from ERIC implementation strategies should be specified in greater detail, including information on how, when, and for what duration individual implementation strategies should be applied. Trial Registration: OSF Registries osf.io/dsrh8; https://osf.io/dsrh8/overview
title: Implementation Strategies for Digital Nursing Technologies in Home Care: Scoping Review

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> High-risk alcohol use and alcohol use disorder (AUD) are significant contributors to surgical risk and complications yet remain underidentified in surgical populations. While electronic health records (EHRs) contain relevant information about patients’ alcohol use in clinical notes, manual chart review is time-intensive and impractical at scale. Natural language processing (NLP) offers a path to automated identification, but alcohol-related risk classes are highly imbalanced in clinical populations, making multiclass classification particularly challenging. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aims to develop an automated NLP pipeline for 4-class alcohol risk classification using clinical notes in a surgical population, addressing class imbalance by leveraging intermediate annotation evidence generated during the human labeling process. <strong>Methods:</strong> We manually labeled 1000 surgical patients drawn from a large academic health system into ordinal alcohol risk classes (no-alcohol, low-risk, high-risk, and probable-dependence) and a fifth class indicating no mention of alcohol use. We used a structured annotation process with 6 trained annotators and expert-developed guidelines. We developed a multistage NLP pipeline operating on 3 years of clinical notes per patient. First, a rules-based preprocessing stage filtered notes to clinically relevant sections containing alcohol-related content. No-mention cases were excluded from further modeling. Second, a BioClinicalBERT-based multilabel classifier (“auto-annotator”) was fine-tuned to reproduce the annotations created by human labelers at the section level, producing a structured 26-dimensional probability vector for each section. Finally, a bidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) network classified patients into the 4 risk categories by processing each patient’s ordered sequence of auto-annotation vectors, allowing the model to capture temporally accumulating evidence across clinical encounters. <strong>Results:</strong> Human annotators achieved 93.7% first-pass agreement overall (Fleiss κ=0.8891), but agreement was as low as 67.5% for probable-dependence cases. The 4-class LSTM classifier achieved a weighted-average <i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score of 0.86 and a macroaverage <i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score of 0.77 on a held-out validation set of 195 patients. One-vs-rest area under the curve (AUC) scores were 0.97 for no-alcohol, 0.88 for low-risk, 0.90 for probable-dependence, and 0.71 for high-risk. Collapsed to a binary high/low risk classification, the model achieved an accuracy of 0.92 and a macro-<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score of 0.80. Performance was comparable across biological sex without explicit sex-specific training. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> We used a 2-stage NLP pipeline to identify 4 ordinal classes of alcohol use risk in surgical patients. Four-class alcohol-use classification presents a highly imbalanced problem that constrains the availability of high-importance but rare labels in the dataset. We addressed this data scarcity by using intermediate annotation evidence as well as final labels to enrich the feature space for the classification task. The pipeline was able to separate patient records into 4 strata of alcohol-use risk, with “high-risk” patients being most likely to be misclassified into an adjacent class.
title: Natural Language Processing Supported by Annotation Process Artifacts to Detect Risky Alcohol Use in Electronic Health Records: Algorithm Development and Validation Study

summary: This study outlines an approach through sampling design and post hoc weighting adjustments to execute a polysubstance use–focused survey with applied bias reduction techniques at lower cost.
title: Sequential Surveying Within Existing Studies to Advance Research Expeditiously

summary: Background: Remote consultations, including telephone, video, text, or web-based consultations, are now common in sexual and reproductive health services in England and Wales, offering convenience and efficiency but also raising concerns about the safeguarding of service users compared with in-person care. While guidance exists, evidence on how safeguarding is enacted remotely is limited. Objective: This research examines how safeguarding is managed remotely in sexual and reproductive health services, including associated challenges, benefits, and perceptions of acceptability. As part of the Connect study (NIHR153151), qualitative data were collected across 3 diverse case study areas in England and Wales. Methods: Semistructured interviews were conducted with service users/potential service users and professional stakeholders, who were recruited using maximum variation sampling through multiple recruitment methods, including clinic-based approaches, established networks, email and text invitations, and the Connect study website (March 2024-January 2025). Data were thematically analyzed using inductive and deductive approaches. A total of 89 interviews were conducted with 54 service users/potential service users and 35 professional stakeholders across the 3 study sites. Results: Four themes were identified: (1) challenges of delivering remote safeguarding in practice, (2) importance of a safe space for patients, (3) limitations of a one-size-fits-all approach, and (4) strategies to support remote safeguarding. Participants reported challenges, including limited access to visual cues, variable comfort with disclosure, and privacy concerns. Professional stakeholders used adaptive approaches to build trust, ensure safety, and tailor safeguarding to individual circumstances, emphasizing that effective remote safeguarding relies on clinician judgment and sensitive communication. Conclusions: Remote consultations offer flexibility, but safeguarding depends on access to a safe, private space. Those with language barriers or limited ability to create such a space at home, such as people experiencing housing instability or coercive control, may have greater safeguarding needs. Ensuring access to in-person options, clear safeguarding protocols, and appropriate clinician training is essential to address these challenges.
title: Safeguarding During Remote Sexual and Reproductive Health Consultations in England and Wales: Qualitative Study

summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on medical specialty board multiple-choice questions (MCQs) but underperform in complex medical reasoning. This gap indicates a need to improve LLM medical reasoning and evaluation paradigms. Objective: This study aimed to develop and evaluate MedEvalArena, a dynamically regenerable benchmark for assessing medical reasoning in LLMs. Methods: In a symmetric round-robin format, 6 frontier LLMs from the OpenAI, Grok, Gemini, Claude, Kimi, and DeepSeek families generated challenging board-style medical MCQs, adjudicated question validity on an ensemble LLM-as-judge panel, and answered the validated examination. Candidate items were generated until each model contributed 50 validated questions according to Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC)/American Board of Medical Specialties (ABMS) physician specialty distributions, yielding a 300-question examination. Judges adjudicated candidate questions’ logical validity and medical accuracy. We compared question-generation validity rates, assessed leave-one-out judge agreement, and tested for self-judging preference. Questions were audited for overlap with public MedQA (medical question-answering) benchmarks. We tested question-answering (QA) accuracy across LLMs using a binomial-logit generalized linear mixed model likelihood-ratio test. A generator-stratified 90-question subset was completed by 5 board-certified physicians for paired human-LLM analysis. We evaluated inference cost-accuracy tradeoffs. Multiple comparisons were adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure. Results: Judge-panel validity rates were significantly higher for questions generated by OpenAI (94.8%, Wilson 95% CI 85.9%-98.2%), Gemini (92.3%, 95% CI 83.2%-96.7%), and Claude (83.3%, 95% CI 72.6%-90.4%) models than those generated by Kimi (63.8%, 95% CI 54.3%-72.4%), Grok (56%, 95% CI 45.8%-65.8%), and DeepSeek (46.0%, 95% CI 37.4%-54.7%). Kimi also demonstrated significantly higher validity than DeepSeek (2-sample tests of proportions; BH-adjusted =.01). The public-source similarity audit found no exact or near-duplicate matches. Leave-one-out judge agreement was moderate. Generator-specific same-family judging coefficients were nonnegative (0 to 11.0 percentage points); however, none remained significant after BH adjustment. There was no significant difference between the 6 frontier LLM QA accuracies, which ranged from 85.7% (257/300) to 91.7% (275/300), on the 300-question examination (generalized linear mixed model likelihood-ratio test =.07). The study had 80% power to detect LLM accuracy differences of 9.2 percentage points; nonsignificance did not establish equivalence. On the 90-question subset, physician accuracy was 85.6% (95% CI 79.4%‐91.7%; stratified normal with finite-population correction), compared with aggregate LLM performance of 94.4% (85/90; Wilson 95% CI 87.6%‐97.6%). This difference was not significant (McNemar test, =.08); however, the study was powered to detect a human vs LLM accuracy difference of 14% to 15%. Answering-only costs varied by nearly 2 orders of magnitude, with multiple models on the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier. Conclusions: MedEvalArena enables scalable, regenerable, peer-judged benchmarking of LLM medical reasoning. Question-generation validity differentiated model families more clearly than answering accuracy, suggesting that valid MCQ generation may complement QA benchmarks for assessing LLM medical reasoning.
title: Medical Reasoning in Large Language Models: Development and Evaluation of the MedEvalArena Benchmark

summary: Clinical AI is moving from systems that generate discrete predictions and recommendations toward agents capable of pursuing clinical objectives through repeated tool use, communication, planning, and state-changing actions. Emerging systems support multistep electronic health record workflows, and increasingly envision longitudinal care across repeated encounters. This transition expands safety assessment beyond discrete outputs and actions. Through its actions, an agent can help create the clinical state on which its subsequent decisions depend. Consequently, individually defensible actions may compose into an unsafe trajectory, even when no single action is clearly erroneous. We propose recoverability-centered trajectory governance as a clinical synthesis of established safety approaches, linking patient-specific corrective capacity to the continuing justification for delegated authority. Its central objective is clinical recoverability: preserving the opportunity for the human-AI care system to redirect care before clinically acceptable corrective pathways are exhausted. We define recovery margin as the remaining opportunity for such correction, and reauthorization boundaries as conditions requiring delegated authority to end or narrow pending renewed human judgment. This framing distinguishes reversibility, primarily a property of an action, from recoverability, a property of an evolving clinical trajectory. The operational framework combines persistent obligation tracking, independent monitoring, explicit reauthorization, authority contraction, graceful degradation, independent escalation, and verified human takeover. Oversight should concentrate at consequential trajectory junctions. Evaluation should combine trajectory stress testing, component-specific recovery-margin indicators, interruption-and-takeover testing, and population-level surveillance. Trajectory governance complements product lifecycle oversight by examining whether continued patient-specific delegation remains justified as care evolves. Because corrective capacity depends partly on access to timely monitoring and human rescue, recoverability is also an equity issue. The defining safety question is therefore not only whether an action is acceptable but whether continued delegation remains justified. The proposed indicators and governance mechanisms require domain-specific operationalization and empirical validation, including comparison with established safeguards.
title: Recoverability-Centered Trajectory Governance for Long-Horizon Clinical AI Agents

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Antithrombotic stewardship is critical for reducing preventable harm from inappropriate anticoagulant prescribing. Electronic health record (EHR)–embedded clinical decision support (CDS) alerts can prevent prescribing errors at the point of care, but their real-world effectiveness is variable and often limited by alert fatigue and poor workflow integration. Whether augmenting interruptive medication alerts with just‑in‑time access to clinical pharmacists improves prescriber response remains unclear. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to (1) compare the effectiveness of synchronous, interruptive direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) prescribing alerts with and without an embedded clinical pharmacist referral option for correcting inappropriate new prescriptions within 7 days, and (2) evaluate the system‑level impact of implementing synchronous DOAC alerts on inappropriate prescribing over time. <strong>Methods:</strong> We conducted a prescriber‑level randomized comparative effectiveness trial within a large US academic health system. Prescribers who placed an inappropriate ambulatory apixaban or rivaroxaban order were randomized to receive an interruptive EHR alert either with or without an embedded clinical pharmacist referral link. The primary outcome was any change to the prescription within 7 days. In parallel, a system‑level interrupted time series analysis examined weekly proportions of inappropriate DOAC prescriptions (secondary outcomes) from 24 months before through 29 months after alert implementation. Exploratory outcomes included adverse events within 30 days and alert implementation metrics. <strong>Results:</strong> Among 2082 prescribers writing DOAC prescriptions during the study period, 300 (14.4%) triggered at least one inappropriate prescription and were randomized; after prespecified exclusions, 758 alerts across 286 prescribers were analyzed. Overall, 28.9% (219/758) of alerts led to a prescription change within 7 days. The proportion of alerts leading to a prescription change did not differ between alerts with and without pharmacist referral (difference 1 percentage point [95% CI −7 to 9]). The system‑wide proportion of inappropriate DOAC prescriptions exhibited a significant downward preimplementation trend (−0.04 percentage points per week [95% CI −0.06 to −0.02]), followed by an immediate 3.5‑percentage‑point absolute reduction at alert launch (to 9.7%), with no subsequent slope change. Adverse events within 30 days were uncommon and similar across arms. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Adding an embedded pharmacist referral option to an interruptive DOAC prescribing alert did not increase short‑term prescription changes. However, the implementation of synchronous, user-centered alerts was associated with a system-level reduction in inappropriate DOAC prescribing. These findings support a complementary digital stewardship model in which high‑value, point‑of‑order alerts prevent routine prescribing errors, while clinical pharmacists focus on complex and longitudinal medication management. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong> ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05351749; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05351749
title: Use of Synchronous, Interruptive Electronic Health Record–Embedded Medication Alerts to Improve Evidence-Based Medication Prescribing: Randomized Comparative Effectiveness Trial of Two Prescriber Alerts

summary: This Viewpoint argues that measurement design, not model capability, is the first constraint on clinical AI in acute inpatient psychiatry and proposes intentional sufficiency as a design rule for sleep sensing on acute wards. Acute psychiatric wards exclude much of the conventional sensing design space: ligature, ingestion, and projectile hazards; unreliable adherence; impaired consent; and nursing workload mean that a device that is excellent when a patient is cooperative may be absent when the patient is most unwell. We define intentional sufficiency in 3 parts: the intended clinical use sets the required signal properties and acceptable error; safety, validity, consent, and workflow constraints define the feasible design space; and within that space, the rule selects the least burdensome option that preserves the required properties, because excess capability can be paid for in persistence, not only in money. We contrast this rule with capability-maximizing design using 2 examples at opposite ends of the design space: a structured nightly nursing sleep duration record that, in Taiwan, already exists within routine care, and a disposable wrist-worn sensing architecture under development that reduces the wearable to what the derived sleep measure requires. The first shows when the rule can conclude that no hardware should be added, provided adequacy has been shown for the intended use; the second shows when it concludes that hardware must be redesigned, and is presented as a design prediction rather than a result. Importantly, agreement with a reference method does not by itself establish task-level sufficiency; greater sensing capability does not necessarily produce more clinically available information when deployment and persistence are constrained; and some signal properties are validity defining and cannot be traded against cost.
title: Measure the Ward First: Intentional Sufficiency as a Design Rule for Sleep Sensing in Acute Inpatient Psychiatry

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Correct use of a pressurized metered-dose inhaler (pMDI), usually with a valved holding chamber, depends on use-related conditions that caregivers may not observe directly, including inhalation pattern, actuation-inhalation timing, mask seal, and device orientation. Many digital inhaler systems emphasize actuation or adherence. Systems that infer technique-related conditions from proxy signals may add real-time feedback but also create false reassurance if a positive state is displayed when evidence is inadequate. Caregiver expectations for such feedback and its failure states remain poorly characterized before prototype development. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to characterize caregivers' experiences of pediatric inhaler administration and translate responses to a proposed sensor concept into traceable candidate safety, system, and validation requirements. <strong>Methods:</strong> We conducted 23 semistructured concept-elicitation sessions through Zoom videoconference with 27 caregivers of children who currently or previously used a pMDI. Interviews consisted of 19 individual and 4 dyadic sessions pairing 2 caregivers from different households. Sessions were conducted remotely between April and July 2026 from the University of Calgary, Alberta, Canada. Recruitment originated in Calgary and was not geographically restricted. A 6-phase guide examined current practices, difficulties, prior digital-tool use, and responses to a screen-shared clip-on concept incorporating airflow-, timing-, seal-, and orientation-related sensing; on-device feedback; an optional child-facing app; and a caregiver dashboard. No working prototype was evaluated. Approximately 86,000 transcript words underwent hybrid directed and conventional qualitative content analysis using an 18-category codebook. Two researchers independently coded the complete 27×18 matrix (486 paired decisions) across 2 rounds. Consensus categories were translated into candidate requirements and assigned an earliest verification or evaluation locus. Counts are descriptive caregiver-voice tallies, not prevalence estimates. <strong>Results:</strong> Persistent uncertainty about whether administration conditions were adequate was the dominant lived experience (19/27); for 5 caregivers, existing passive cues had not resolved it. A simple, real-time on-device signal was endorsed by 25 caregivers, but willingness to consider the concept was conditional on reliability (9 caregivers named reasons for abandonment, notably a “false green”), low-friction operation during acute symptoms (12/27), minimal added bulk and technique change, and one or more of clinical validation, clinician recommendation, or a trial pathway (composite category; 23/27). Stances on gamification (20/27), dashboard cadence (18/27), aesthetics (24/27), and privacy (18/27) supported an optional, configurable software layer. Intercoder agreement was 94% (Cohen κ=0.88). The analytic synthesis yielded a conceptual architecture separating observable proxy signals, an inference and data-quality gate, and positive, corrective, or uncertain feedback states. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Participating caregivers prioritized immediate and interpretable feedback about use-related conditions. The findings support conservative state assignment, an explicit uncertain state for indeterminate signals, and app-independent acute-use feedback. These are candidate requirements rather than validated device specifications; subsequent work should proceed through bench verification, simulated-use human factors evaluation, and prospective clinical or field validation.
title: Caregiver-Informed Safety and System Requirements for Real-Time Feedback During Pediatric Inhaler Use: Qualitative Concept-Elicitation Study
